issues.description: The manuscript treats a 10-item pairwise discrimination task as a rigorous measure of causal understanding, but the optimization problem itself requires integrating the tradeoff between moment of inertia and centre of mass simultaneously. Judging which of two wheels is faster when only one factor varies can be solved by heuristic discrimination and does not establish mechanistic or multidimensional causal understanding. This threatens the central claim that technology improved without understanding, because the operationalization does not fully match the theoretical construct.
issues.quote: This allowed us to rigorously measure participants’ causal understanding of the system after they completed their 5 trials (Figure 1.E). Participants’ understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails. ... The test comprised 10 pairs of wheels: 5 in which wheels varied in their moment of inertia, 5 in which wheels varied in the position of their centre of mass.

issues.description: The preregistered plan distinguished understanding of inertia and centre of mass, but the reported analysis collapses them into a single aggregate score precisely because they were negatively correlated. Aggregating negatively related subscales can cancel theoretically meaningful differences and make a null overall effect appear where dimension-specific effects exist. This directly affects the headline conclusion that understanding did not improve.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated (Supplementary Figure 9 and Supplementary Table 7) and some individuals better understood inertia than centre of mass while others better understood centre of mass than inertia (Figure 3I and Supplementary Figure 2). As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly concludes that optimization occurred without causal understanding, but the data presented indicate partial understanding rather than its absence. Participants scored above random-guessing levels and the discussion acknowledges that they had 'appropriate intuitions'. The findings support, at most, incomplete or non-improving explicit understanding—not that causal understanding was absent or unnecessary in a strong sense.
issues.quote: our experiment shows that highly optimized technologies can emerge from the accumulation of many improvements made across generations linked by cultural transmission, without the need for an accurate causal understanding of the system.

issues.description: The claim that theory transmission had 'no noticeable effect' is stronger than the evidence warrants. The treatment and interaction intervals are wide and include substantively meaningful positive and negative values. This is absence of precise evidence, not strong evidence of absence. Given only 14 independent chains per treatment, the study is not well positioned to support a null conclusion.
issues.quote: Results show that the average wheel speed increased at a similar rate in the "Configurations + Theory" as it did in the "Configurations" treatment (Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h, Figure 2.A) ... Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.description: No a priori power analysis or precision justification is provided. The appeal to prior studies having smaller samples is not a substitute for showing that this design has enough independent units to detect the effects being interpreted, especially treatment-by-generation interactions and null effects.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31.

issues.description: The 'Configurations + Theory' condition differs from the control in more than one way: participants both receive a theory and are required to generate one themselves, and they do so before the understanding assessment is completed. Any treatment difference could therefore be due to self-explanation/verbalization, receiving a theory, or both. The design does not isolate the effect of transmitted theory.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system. Participants were asked to write their theory before the test phase was completed.

issues.description: The study frames the manipulation as transmission of causal models, but the transmitted theory is heavily restricted: short text only, fixed sentence stem, and no transmission of configuration-performance details. This may artificially weaken the usefulness of theory transmission and makes it difficult to generalize from this manipulation to richer real-world theory teaching or explanation.
issues.quote: Participants could not transmit information about the performance of a specific configuration in order to prevent individuals from extending the number of transmitted configurations as compared to the “Configurations” treatment.  Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with “The wheel covers the distance faster when...”.

issues.description: The exploratory analyses sort participants by the kind of theory they inherited and then use causal language such as 'increased' and 'decreased'. But these theory categories were not randomly assigned; they are endogenous products of prior participants and chain histories. Therefore, the reported subgroup differences cannot support causal claims about the effects of inheriting a given type of theory.
issues.quote: Inheriting an inertia-related theory increased their understanding of inertia, but decreased their understanding of centre of mass; symmetrically, inheriting a centre-of-mass-related theory increased their understanding of centre of mass, but decreased their understanding about inertia.

issues.description: Participants in the theory condition always inherited both configurations and theories. Because the content of a theory is likely correlated with the configurations it accompanies, observed differences attributed to theory may actually reflect the inherited wheel examples or their performance. The analyses do not appear to control for inherited configurations when interpreting theory-specific effects.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations” treatment (n = 70), the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in the chain were provided to the next participant in the chain. In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

issues.description: Although analyses are described as preregistered, the final model was chosen after comparing several candidate models on fit to the observed data. The manuscript does not specify the candidate set, selection criterion, or whether this procedure was itself preregistered. This introduces researcher degrees of freedom and weakens confirmatory interpretation.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.description: The analysis plan was changed after seeing the data because the preregistered model did not converge. The replacement analysis drops a theoretically central variable and changes the outcome from separate principle scores to an aggregate. Without prespecified fallback rules or sensitivity analyses, this substantially increases analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.description: The experimenter knew condition assignment during data collection, and the analyst was also unblinded. Because the experimenter manually positioned weights and ran sessions, and because analysis choices changed post hoc, lack of blinding increases the risk of expectancy effects and biased analytic decisions.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments. ... Data analyses were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.description: Non-descending wheels are handled inconsistently across analyses: one analysis restricts data to reduce their occurrence, another assigns them a speed of 0, and the figure displays average speed only for non-failure wheels. Because failures are an important part of performance, inconsistent coding can materially change estimates and make within- and between-treatment results not directly comparable.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset. ... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.description: The manuscript uses linear models for outcomes that are not naturally Gaussian: understanding is a bounded discrete score, and speed includes a pile-up at zero from failed wheels and an upper bound near the apparatus maximum. Without justification or model checking, Gaussian linear models may misrepresent variance, uncertainty, and effect sizes.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable ... We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable ... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.description: The recorded descent interval is described as 92 cm between switches, yet speed is later described as 1 m divided by descent time. Unless an unreported correction was applied, this implies a systematic mismatch in speed computation, payoff calibration, and the stated maximum possible speed.
issues.quote: Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails ... The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations

issues.description: The methods say inference used Bayesian credible intervals/HPDIs, but the results repeatedly label intervals as confidence intervals. This conflates frequentist and Bayesian inferential terminology and makes the statistical reporting internally inconsistent.
issues.quote: Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences. ... Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h

issues.description: The understanding test offers three response options, but the manuscript does not state how responses were scored, whether 'No difference' was ever a correct answer, or what exact score constitutes chance performance. This omission makes the reported scores, 'better than chance' statements, and replication of the measure difficult to evaluate.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”. ... Horizontal line shows expected score for random guessers.

issues.description: All participants received the same item order in the understanding test. This allows order effects, learning during the test, fatigue, or carryover from earlier items to influence scores. Counterbalancing or randomization would be preferable for an outcome intended to index understanding.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: Key exploratory claims are based on very small and uneven subgroups, particularly the 'full theory' group (N = 6). Such small, post hoc subgroups produce unstable estimates and are especially problematic when participants are nested in chains and no formal multilevel analysis of these subgroup comparisons is reported.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the “Configurations + Theory” treatment except first-generation participants), 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.description: The study used exclusively single-sex chains, yet the discussion claims the findings generalize to mixed-gender collaborative settings. No mixed-gender condition was tested, so this statement is unsupported.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.description: The data come from French university students performing a simple laboratory wheel task with immediate feedback and constrained written messages. Extrapolating from this design to the interpretation of complex archaeological technologies and human technological evolution is a substantial overreach that is not warranted by the sample or task.
issues.quote: our experiment indicates that one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities (such as reasoning, problem-solving or planning), since these abilities are not the sole driver of technological sophistication 1,9.

issues.description: The argument that a low-dimensional optimization problem is a 'conservative test' for claims about complex technologies is conceptually backwards. Low-dimensional tasks are generally easier to optimize via trial-and-error and social learning, and easier to understand than high-dimensional real technologies. Success in this task therefore does not conservatively establish the same for more complex technologies such as bows.
issues.quote: Finally, although the physics of the system are by no means trivial, the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses, compared to the many-dimensional problem of optimizing, for example, the performance of a bow 13.

issues.description: Both experimental treatments involve social transmission; the study lacks a no-transmission/asocial control condition. Without such a control, the manuscript cannot cleanly isolate how much of the generational improvement is due to social transmission itself versus procedural drift, temporal effects, or other between-session differences.
issues.quote: Two treatments were run. ... All participants except those in the first generation were provided with social information.

issues.description: Although inter-rater reliability is reported, the manuscript does not explain how disagreements among the three coders were resolved or how final categories were assigned to each theory. Because later analyses depend on these coded theory categories, the absence of a reproducible decision rule limits evaluation and replication.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel (i.e. the respective role of inertia and centre of mass in the performance of the wheel) and were asked to code participants’ theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass. ... Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).
